summary: Defines a MIB module for managing SONET and SDH interfaces, the optical transmission systems carriers use. It is a companion to the DS1/E1 and DS3/E3 MIB documents. It obsoletes RFC 1595 and was replaced by RFC 3592.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a standard set of gauges for the fast fiber-optic lines of phone companies, so any monitoring program can read them.

subtitle: A standard way to monitor high-speed optical transmission lines using SNMP.

tldr.problem: Telecommunications carriers need a standard way to monitor SONET and SDH optical transmission systems, tracking performance, errors, and the status of connections at multiple layers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2558 defines SNMP MIB objects for SONET/SDH interfaces, organized by transmission layer (section, line, path, virtual tributary). It tracks current and historical performance metrics including error counts, defects, and failures.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can use standard SNMP monitoring to detect and troubleshoot problems on high-speed optical links. RFC 3592 superseded this specification.

today: RFC 2558 is a Proposed Standard. It was superseded by RFC 3592. The SONET/SDH MIB remains central to the management and monitoring of carrier transmission networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2558 defines a portion of the SNMP Management Information Base for SONET/SDH interfaces—the high-speed optical transmission systems used by telecommunications carriers. SONET is the North American standard (Synchronous Optical Network); SDH is the equivalent international standard (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy).

The MIB is a companion to earlier documents covering DS1/E1 (lower-speed lines) and DS3/E3 interfaces. It extends the basic SNMP interface management framework (ifTable) with SONET/SDH-specific metrics for monitoring performance and troubleshooting optical links.
sections.plainLanguage: SONET and SDH are the super-fast fiber-optic lines that carry phone calls and data across long distances. This document explains what numbers a monitoring system should read to keep tabs on these lines.

sections.title: SONET/SDH Architecture
sections.content:
SONET/SDH uses a layered architecture. From bottom to top: the Physical Medium is the actual fiber; the Section Layer regenerates and monitors signals across a single span between regenerators; the Line Layer manages the entire link between two endpoints; and the Path Layer carries traffic across multiple links end-to-end. Within paths, Virtual Tributaries (VTs) in SONET (or Virtual Containers (VCs) in SDH) multiplex lower-speed signals.

SONET designates speeds as STS-N (Synchronous Transport Signal, where N is the multiplicity): STS-1 is 51.84 Mbps, STS-3 is 155.52 Mbps, STS-12 is 622.08 Mbps, and so on. One STS-3c (concatenated) carries one path, while an STS-12 may carry four STS-3c paths. Each path can multiplex many VT1.5s (1.728 Mbps) or VT2s.

The MIB represents each SONET/SDH layer as a separate interface entry (ifEntry) in the standard ifTable, with the ifStackTable tracking how layers nest and multiplex together.
sections.plainLanguage: SONET is organized like an organization chart. The fiber is the company, sections are regions, lines are divisions, paths are departments, and virtual tributaries are teams. This RFC defines what to measure at each level.

sections.title: Performance Metrics
sections.content:
RFC 2558 defines performance objects for current and historical (interval) statistics at each layer. Current statistics are for the ongoing interval; interval statistics cover 15-minute buckets (with the current interval plus up to 96 prior intervals maintained).

Key metrics include Coding Violations (CVs)—bit errors detected by Bit Interleaved Parity (BIP) checking; Errored Seconds (ES)—seconds with one or more CVs or defects; and Severely Errored Seconds (SES)—seconds with a high number of CVs or one or more defects. The MIB also tracks Unavailable Seconds (UAS): time the interface is down, declared after 10 contiguous SESs and cleared after 10 good seconds.

The threshold for SES varies by standard (ANSI T1.231-1993, T1.231-1997, or ITU-T G.826-1995), so RFC 2558 adds an object to specify which threshold set an implementation uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB counts errors, bad seconds, very bad seconds, and down time. Each level of the network has its own counters so you can see where problems happen.

sections.title: Defects and Failures
sections.content:
SONET/SDH signals include overhead bytes that carry control information and error flags. When these signals become corrupted or absent, specific defects are declared. Loss of Signal (LOS) occurs when no transitions are detected on the incoming signal (millisecond timescales). Loss of Frame (LOF) is declared when the frame alignment is lost (3 millisecond timescale).

Higher-layer defects include Loss of Pointer (LOP), which signals that the path or VT pointer cannot be found within eight consecutive frames; Alarm Indication Signal (AIS), which alerts downstream equipment to an upstream failure; and Remote Defect Indication (RDI) (also called FERF, Far End Receive Failure), which signals a problem detected by the far end. Each defect has specific timing criteria for declaration and clearing, typically 2.5 +/- 0.5 seconds.

The MIB tracks the current status at each layer (whether it is defect-free or which defect is present) and counts error types per 15-minute interval.
sections.plainLanguage: Defects are specific problems: no signal, lost frame alignment, lost path pointer, alarm signals, and far-end failure alerts. The MIB watches for these and counts them.

sections.title: MIB Objects and Tables
sections.content:
The MIB defines eight major object groups: the Medium Group (physical medium properties), the Section Group (current and interval statistics), the Line Group (current and interval), the Far End Line Group (what the far end reports), the Path Group (current and interval), the Far End Path Group, the VT Group, and the Far End VT Group.

Each group has a 'Current' table for real-time metrics and an 'Interval' table for historical 15-minute buckets. The Medium Group also includes loopback configuration (to enable diagnostic loopbacks) and a Circuit Identifier field (for vendor troubleshooting).

Two optional features allow implementations to choose: they can either perform retroactive adjustments to counters when entering/exiting unavailable time, or delay updates in a queue as specified in Appendix A of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has organized tables: one for the physical medium, one for each network layer (section, line, path, VT), with separate tables for current status and 15-minute snapshots.

sections.title: Revisions and Conformance
sections.content:
RFC 2558 obsoletes RFC 1595 (published in 1994). Major changes include improved textual conventions for performance counters, a loopback configuration object, the addition of the SES threshold set selector, per-interval data validity flags, and conformance information reorganization.

The MIB defines four conformance levels: basic (section and line layers), line and association (adds far-end line), path (adds path and far-end path), and full (all groups including VT and far-end VT). Implementations can choose the level appropriate for their equipment.
sections.plainLanguage: The 1994 version was updated in 1999 with better error handling, loopback controls, and conformance levels so different equipment vendors can implement what they need.
